Well, Mr. Chairman, I gave the hon, gentlman the courtesy of the floor, and this is the sort of thing we always get from that quarter. Let me quote from one who probably has as much knowledge of the United States as the hon. member for Davenport; I refer to Woodrow Wilson, who brought into being a federal reserve system in the hope that it might cure the situation that existed in that country. In 1911, before he was president, Woodrow Wilson pointed out:
The great monopoly of this country is the money monopoly. So long as that exists, our old variety and freedom and individual energy of development are out of the question. The growth of the nation and all our activities are in the hands of a few men who, by reason of their own limitations chill, check and destroy genuine economic freedom.
Wilson made a great attempt at monetary reform in the establishment of the federal reserve system; but Elihu Root, one of the greatest lawyers who ever sat in the United States senate, said:
This bill (the Federal Reserve Act) proposes to put in pawn the credit of the United States. We are setting our steps in the pathway that brought Rome to its fall.
That was because the federal reserve system was a bankers' system, owned by bankers and controlled by bankers, and not owned and controlled by the government of the United States. That was what Roosevelt found also when he came to power; but before that, President Hoover had something to say about the situation that existed in the disastrous years from 1928 to 1932, when he was president. This is what he said:
I stated that this depression has exposed many weaknesses in our economic system. It has shown much wrongdoing. There has been exploitation and abuse of financial power. These weaknesses must be corrected and that wrongdoing must be punished.
The American people must have protection from insecure banking through a stronger system. They must be relieved from conditions which permit the credit machinery of the

Supply-Finance
country to be made available without adequate check for wholesale speculation in securities, with its ruinous consequences to millions of our citizens and to national recovery. This the federal reserve system has proved incapable of doing. I recommend to congress the sane reform of our banking laws.
Let me now quote from another man who is somewhat conversant with American history.
I refer to President Roosevelt who, in one of the first speeches to congress after his election, said:
Nature still offers her bounty, and human efforts have multiplied it. Plenty is at our door-step but a generous use of it languishes in the very sight of the supply. Primarily this is because the rulers of the exchange of mankind's goods have failed through their own incompetence. Practices of the unscrupulous money changers stand indicted in the court of public opinion, rejected by the hearts and minds of men.
Stripped of the lure of profit by which to induce our people to follow their false leadership, they have proposed only the lending of more money.
They have resorted to exhortations, pleading tearfully for restored confidence. They know only the rules of a generation of self-seekers. They have no vision and where there is no vision the people perish.
The money changers have fled from their high seats in the temple of our civilization. We may now restore that temple to the ancient truths.
Let me now call as a witness another British statesman and what he had to say about Roosevelt when he tackled the problem of reforming the banking system of the United States. He has gone a long way beyond the point where Woodrow Wilson laid down his great work. Speaking of Roosevelt's attack on the bankers, Lloyd George said:
The intrepidity with which he is fighting against the machinations of the established and arrogant priesthood of the golden calf is being watched with a thrill of admiration by those who, all the World over, have been suffering from its thraldom. If he wins he will have rendered a service to mankind which will exceed that of Lincoln when he abolished a more limited slavery.
But his task is even more formidable, for the hierachy he has challenged is powerful and its janissaries in all lands are federated in a well-knit, well-drilled and well-equipped brotherhood in arms. They play into each other's hands-they fight each other's battles. If they fail, they will share each other's ruin-if they succeed, they will divide the loot among themselves.
In London and in Paris they are unassailably entrenched. To adopt the scriptural quotation, "Judas is their law giver. Industry is their wash-pot and over successive ministries have they cast their shoe."
I am not calling witnesses from the rabble rousers; I am calling as witnesses for this cause the statesmen of the world; and let no man iu this house ever again say that I am
bringing forward my own ideas. The ideas I have offered on this great question are not mine. They belong to men infinitely more capable than I, men of established position not merely in economic academic thinking but in the world of political history.
Let me now come to our own house; hon. members probably will recall these words:
Once a nation parts with the control of its currency and credit it matters not who makes the nation's laws.	,
Usury once in control will wreck any nation. Until the control of the issue of currency and credit is restored to government, and recognized as its most conspicuous and sacred responsibility all talk of the sovereignty of parliament and of democracy is idle and futile.
That was saidi by the then leader of the opposition speaking in the house in opposition to the Bank of Canada bill, establishing the Bank of Canada as a privately-owned institution. That leader of the opposition is now Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Mackenzie King).
Supporting his then leader in opposition, now the Prime Minister, the present Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) made this declaration:
The control of credit and currency is the biggest and most important public utility in the activities of the nation. The central bank is a public utility, and the citizens should not relinquish control of its administration.
I am not one who necessarily champions public ownership at all times and in -all places, but there are certain things that should be under public ownership or public control, and certainly the very first and most important of these is the institution which controls, which guides, which directs the whole economic life of the nation.
I could quote many more-many men equally distinguished. In an ordinary- case at law I never would have to call as great an array of witnesses men who were experts upon the basis of their actual experience to secure a verdict than those men whose statements I have placed before the committee tonight.
No; these' ideas are not mine. I would not. think of asking my colleagues in parliament to consider any view I might have on so important an issue as national currency, were I not able to sustain and support that view out of the wisdom of the ages, and out of the- plain actual experience of reason and common sense. No; they are not my views.
There is one other statement the minister made. He said, "We are doing what England is doing." I want to say this: One of the great mistakes we have made in the economy of Canada has been our attempt to appropriate an economy which is successfully applied in England, but which does not apply to Canada at all. Canada is a nation with an abundance of resources and a dearth of
Supply-Finance

people. England is a nation with an abundance of people and a dearth of resources. Canada has an abundance of things to create and export. England depends upon her foreign trade, and must bring in, industrialize and ship out again. England's financial situation is not similar to ours, nor can what is good for England be accepted as good for Canada.
Let me point this out to the committee. A little while ago orthodox financial experts told us that we had to stick to gold, or we would lose our credit in the markets of London and New York. We were told that unless we maintained that credit we would not be able to get from the accumulated savings of the world the means by which we alone could build our railways, our schools, our hospitals, our communities, and all the things tending to the development of a young country which had not accumulated savings.
A miraculous change has taken place. Today we have assumed a war obligation for this year that is eleven times greater in money value than was the war obligation of the last year of the war of 1914-18. We are spending in 1943-44 about five thousand million dollars. The budget in 1917-18 was S450,000,000. We are financing this ourselves. But on top of that we have said we will finance a contribution to the war of England, to the war of China and of Russia to the value of another billion dollars. We are not going to New York. We are not going to London, for either money or credit. Canada has a bank which the people own, and a banking system that has proven that it can accept and fulfil that burden with Canadian capital. Let no one ever say again that the development of the Dominion of Canada is dependent upon the will of international bankers resident in New York and London.
There is one other statement, the answer to which I should like to have on the record, namely the statement that we know what we are doing. I am not questioning the ability of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) or his advisers; but with the greatest of respect to them I say that in the matter of finance so far as this war is concerned we are moving in uncharted seas. A great job is being done, and we are proving that we can do things in the realm of finance we never dreamed we could do. But mark the difference between this war and the last one. In the last war we went along firmly convinced that victory would be ours, and confident that we would make the defeated nations pay every dollar of cost that the war would involve. We tried to impose those costs in the terms of the peace treaty. Reparations were set up. What did we find? We found that in the very 
imposition of those money obligations were the roots, the seeds, of the disasters which happened in the years of peace, and which eventually grew into another disastrous war.
We have no such conception as that. Today our statesmen are declaring that the power of Germany, Japan, and Italy must be completely destroyed. Does anyone think for one moment we shall take reparations out of those destroyed nations to liquidate the enormous cost of this war? No such idea prevails anywhere. We are therefore assuming obligations which cannot be carried with safety and security unless we bend the best ability and understanding we have to see to it that, when victory comes, the men who have won that victory and the people who have made their contributions in sacrifice are not to be shackled and enslaved by a load of unpayable debt.
There is no danger of our being unable to finance the maximum of the productive capacity and fighting power of the resources and materials that we in Canada possess.
I wish to say in conclusion that whether or not we agree with the policy of the minister, hon. members not only on this side but in all parts of the house must be solidly behind the administration until the fight is won. But that should not deny us the right to offer for consideration ideas which in our opinion may make some contribution to the better understanding and better solution of the problems which face us. So far as I am concerned, I offer what I have to offer in that sense, and with the understanding that if my suggestions can be of any value- to the ministry I hope they will be accepted. If they are not accepted I shall not be deterred in the least iota from giving my wholehearted support to the minister in the work he has to do.

Mr. Chairman, I read in the Financial Post of February 6, 1943, the following statement under the heading "Australian Complaint":
Australia has been highly critical that while Canada supplied certain war material to the United Kingdom free of cost, Britain re-exported the goods for Australian use and charged the Australians in sterling. The Britain arguments were that Australia had considerable sterling balances with which to meet the cost, but the deal rankled none the less.
May I ask the minister whether that statement is true, and if so, what steps have been taken by the Canadian government to correct that state of affairs?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The goods and materials to
the extent of one billion dollars which were contributed to the United Kingdom in. the last fiscal year were contributed without any strings attached. They were based upon an anticipated deficit for the whole sterling area. What arrangements the United Kingdom made with other parts of the sterling area are not known to me. I have heard' the statement made, to which the hon. member has referred. Whether the arrangements between the United Kingdom and Australia are final, whether they are complete or not, I do not know. I am not in a position to state anything about those arrangements. We deal with the United Kingdom as the source of the sterling, as the centre of the sterling area, the dominant partner in that group; and I am unable to give any definite information as to the arrangements which the United Kingdom, government made with the governments of the other parts of the sterling area.
Let me now say this with regard to the future. We are adopting, as the hon. gentleman probably knows, a new principle in the mutual aid bill of this year. It is not to be a gift to the United Kingdom; it is to be a supply of goods-materials, munitions and so forth-to such of the united nations as we think fit to supply from time to time and on such terms as we think fit from time to time; and the situation which is alleged to exist in the excerpt which the hon. gentleman has quoted, and which I cannot affirm or deny, will not exist in the future as far as our contributions are concerned.

Perhaps the minister has
forgotten to answer my question with respect to old age pensions and the possibility of aged parents being able to receive the cost-of-living bonus. The most unfortunate people in Canada to-day in respect of income are the
old age pensioners. A man in receipt of a salary is getting something anyway, although the cost of living has gone up and he is entitled to his bonus and should have it. The old age pensioner cannot earn a living; yet he has to exist on the very small income of $20 a month or less, in some provinces a little more, because some provinces provide an extra five dollars a month; but his earning power has gone, and yet there is no increase for him. The very things which the old age pensioner must have are the things which have risen in price. Take butter, for instance. I do not know how much the price of butter has risen since the war, but it must be somewhere between fifteen and twenty per cent. Or take meat. The price of meat must have increased thirty, forty or even fifty per cent since the outbreak of war. Last winter was an exceptionally hard winter, and while the cost of an extra ton of coal may not mean much to me or to some other man with a fair or even less than average income, to our mothers and fathers who are getting only $20 a month it means the absorption of a veiy large proportion of their monthly income. These old people are in a very unhappy position to-day. Would the minister indicate whether the government is considering the unfortunateness of these people, and can he give the country some hope that the old age pensioner will soon receive at least the cost-of-living bonus?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I have always regarded the cost-of-living bonus as inappropriate to pensioners. The cost-of-living bonus policy is part of our wage policy and is confined to that. As a matter of fact, if the cost-of-living bonus were extended to old age pensioners on the same basis on which it was extended recently to soldiers in respect of their dependents, it would be so small that it would not be satisfactory to anybody. The old age pensioner's problem will have to be met in an entirely different way. A great deal of thought has been given to it. Essentially the question is one of jurisdiction; and the position which this government has taken, and which I announced in November, 1941, is that we regard the responsibility for old age pensions as primarily one of provincial jurisdiction, just to the same extent as mothers' allowances, for example. So that the provinces would not be penalized in any way, so that they would be perfectly free to increase payments to old age pensioners, we offered in November, 1941, to amend the regulations for any province which wished them amended in respect of that province, so that the province itself could pay supplemental allowances to old age pensioners without reducing the amount of the contribution which the dominion government was
Supply-Finance

obligated to make under the dominion act. Several provinces applied for amendment of the regulations, and several provinces are paying supplemental allowances, while others are proposing to do so. I think it is there that the responsibility lies. I hope to see the day when we shall have a contributory old age pension system in this country. We certainly should have it, but we require an amendment of the constitution in order to provide for it, just as we had to have an amendment of the constitution to provide for unemployment insurance. I cannot see why, in a state of affairs where all the provinces have surpluses, and some of them enormous surpluses, the provinces should not undertake this, which is primarily their responsibility, not ours, instead of calling on us, with our huge deficits, running up to two and three thousand million dollars a year.
Despite that fact, I did make this offer in 1941, that if all or substantially all of the provinces requested a reconsideration of the maximum limit in the Old Age Pensions Act, consideration would be given to that request. I did not say that favourable consideration would be given to it; and I am not so sure, in view of the high surplus position of the provinces, that favourable consideration would be given to it. But a start is being made to a certain degree in some of the provinces in accordance with the social views of the people of these provinces-which vary greatly from one province to the other-by the supplemental allowance system.

Before this vote, having to do with the operation of the mint, is earned, will the Minister of Finance tell us what authority he or his department exercises over the closing of branch banks in different part's of the country? Branch banks are to an extent supplementary to the work of the mint, and in some places they have been closed, at great inconvenience to the people whom they formerly served. In my constituency of Cumberland, Springhill, which in 1941 had a population of 7,170 and is now well up to 8,000, with a large population tributary' to Springhill, one of the two banks has been closed recently. We all realize that . extra work is now imposed on the banks all over Canada, and that splendid services are rendered to the Canadian people at this time in spite of reduced staffs. Some bank managers have told me that nearly half of the work which they are doing now is related to the services they perform for the government. They are carrying on under great handicaps, because many of their staffs have enlisted and they have had to take on inexperienced help, including many girls. These banks pay heavy

taxes both to the federal government and to the provincial and municipal governments. In spite of additional duties, in places such as Springhill and in other parts of Canada the banking facilities have been reduced. In the town of Springhill the demands on the banks have been greatly increased, but half the banking facilities have been allowed to close. I should like to ask the minister what authority he or the government exercise over the closing of branch banks in such circumstances.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
We have no authority over the chartered banks. However, at times I do make representations to them in respect of the proposed closing of a branch. I have done that on several occasions, and sometimes the banks have changed their plans in response to my representations; sometimes they do not. I have no power to do anything but make suggestions.
The banks have lost a great many of their young men, who have gone to war. They have tried to replace them by girls, and have been successful to a certain extent, but their man-power problem is a real one. In my judgment it is all right for the banks to close some branches, but for the most part I think they should be city branches rather than rural, because the cities are probably pretty well served, perhaps over-served in some instances. I think the banks have tried to serve the country as best they could. Very often a branch will not be making any money but will be running into a deficit year after year, and naturally the banks want to close such a branch. It is hard for me to press them to keep it open under such conditions, although I have at times urged1 that they give much consideration to the requirements of the community instead of to their own interest from the profit-making point of view.

The Minister of Finance
has taken a definite stand this evening with regard to the responsibility for the payment of old age pensions. He has said that it is primarily the responsibility of the provincial governments. As we all know, the situation is that the Old Age Pensions Act was passed by the dominion, and the dominion has taken the lead throughout. It paid first fifty per cent and now seventy-five per cent of the pensions. Now we come to the position where the pension being paid is not large enough to enable these older people, in many cases, to keep body and soul together. I suggest to the minister that he is dead wrong in taking the stand that it is not the responsibility of this government but of the provincial governments. He has compared the pensions to mothers' allowances, but they are an entirely

Supply-Finance
different type of allowance, paid entirely by the provincial governments and have been so from the start. There should not be any such comparison.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It is not a different type,
though.

This matter is too serious to be just shoved aside in that way. Here is the group of Canadians who are suffering the most on account of the increase in the cost of food, clothing and other necessaries of life. Take for example, the increase in the cost of tea and coffee charged by the restaurants; it has hit many single old age pensioners very hard. The minister should take the lead in meeting the difficulty. He should arrange for a conference of representatives of the dominion and the provinces to review this whole question, including not only giving these people an increase to meet the rise in the cost of living, but also the regulations which in many ways are far too drastic and quite unfair. For example, I think the way in which the income of an aged person is arrived at is quite unfair in many respects; that should be carefully reviewe'd.
Year after year, some of us ask that these changes be made, that this condition be met, but each year we are just pushed aside and the question is shoved off. The matter is far too serious for that. Something should be done to improve the position of these older citizens.

I was rather surprised to hear the statement of the minister to-night as to the policy with reference to old age pensions. We in British Columbia were, I think, the first to bring about the agitation for the establishment of a national act, and I had always thought that the old age pension was one of the great reforms inaugurated by the Liberal party in England in 1906 and that came forward as a great Liberal reform here in 1928. We passed a federal act offering to any province that would come in, to pay half the old age pension up to a ceiling of $20 a month. The theory of that legislation was that in time all the provinces would come in, because it was a reform sponsored and maintained by the national government. It was accepted as a national responsibility by the Conservative administration during the depression, when to relieve the provinces it took over an additional twenty-five per cent, paying seventy-five per cent of any amount paid up to $20 a month.
If we are going to lay down a new Liberal policy, if we are going to repudiate the Liberalism of 1928 and say that this is to become primarily a responsibility of the provinces, that is a retrograde step which I do not believe many Liberals will support.
I know something about these huge provincial surpluses, to which the minister has referred, bookkeeping surpluses, and where they come from They come from two sources: one, the abnormal expenditures of the national government; and the other, the curtailment in expenditures under conditions of war economy practised by every government. Also to some extent they are a product of the efficiency of the accounting department. I have been in politics in British Columbia and in Canada for about thirty-five years. I have heard of nothing but surpluses; I have seen nothing but the steady accumulation of public debt.
Whenever we say to the old age pensioner, you must be thrown upon the care of the provincial administrations because in war time they have surpluses, that would be another step in retrogression, not progress. I do not wish to discuss that more fully now, but I will do so when this matter comes up in its proper place in the estimates. We have either to recognize that a new Liberal policy repudiating that of 1928 is now in operation or to reestablish again the Liberalism of 1928.
In the United States the ceiling is $40 a month, and the federal government there contributes half of what any state government will pay up to that amount. In the state of Washington they have recognized the value of an old age pension not as a mere dole for the aged to live on, but have taken the view that the old age pensioner spending his living allowance is an economic unit of value, circulating throughout the community the medium of exchange that he requires to provide him with a decent standard of living. The old age pensioner takes his poor pittance, even of $40 a month, and spends it. He puts the farmer to work; he puts the local merchant to work; he becomes a consuming employer. We should begin to recognize that our aged are not people whom we should keep in pauperism and bondage but people who in a spirit of goodwill we should convert from liabilities to assets. I speak in this way because I do not think there will be any retrogression on the part of the Liberal party in regard to this matter even in war time.
Let me now add another word. It was a great Liberal reform in England that brought about this change, and it was the Liberals who reduced the age limit in England from seventy to sixty-five years. Mind you, Mr. Chairman, I am heartily in accord with the policy of the government in making a contribution of a billion dollars to the war effort of our allies,
Supply-Finance

but a nation that can find the means of financing such a magnificent contribution to the cause of world freedom can hardly say that we cannot do something for our own needy and aged. Canada must move along with England and the United States. We must get the age limit down to at least that of England; and being as wealthy and as capable of taking care of our people as the United States is, we ought to have at least the same standard that exists across the line.
The question of contributory pensions is not an easy thing to accept. There are a great many people who should enjoy' old age pensions who have no means of making a contribution. What about the wives of the workers? It is true many of them are working to-day', in war time, but does anyone think . that immediately this war is over we shall not attempt to return to the normal life of the nation, when the man will be the labourer and the breadwinner, and the wife and mother will be the custodian of the home? Do not accept contributory' pensions as the solution and do not dismiss the needs.of the aged of Canada to-day on questions of artificial surpluses. Let us never forget that we as a Liberal government have given birth to this great reform and that we have a responsibility to maintain it, as one of the national responsibilities of Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I wish to refer to a few remarks of the hon. member for Vaneouver-Burrard. He says that it is a new policy to state that the responsibility for old age pensions is primarily provincial. That is not correct. I think it has always been admitted by all that the primary responsibility is provincial. That is why provincial governments have the administration of the old age pension system. The dominion government does not administer old age pensions, nor does it pay old age pensions. The dominion government makes contributions to provincial governments, nothing more and nothing less.
We took the first step.
May I ask a question?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext: In view of what the minister has just said, I am wondering whether he has given due consideration to the effect that the increase in old age pensions would have upon our war effort?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It depends upon the increase.

I am thinking of the tens of thousands of old people in this country whose sons are in the armed forces, and whose old age pensions are reduced because those sons make assigned pay to the old folks at home.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Assignment of pay does not reduce old age pensions.
Yes, it does.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, it does not. There was an amendment made some months ago to the old age pensions regulations providing that assigned pay is not to be regarded as income to bring about a reduction of old age pensions.
Is that so in respect of dependents' allowances?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, that is different. Dependents' allowances are certainly income. Assigned pay with dependents' allowances are income-but not assigned pay alone.
But where there are dependents' allowances with assigned pay, they are counted?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

I am thinking of the effect this condition has upon the boys themselves, in the armed forces. I have come in contact with scores of them who feel that their parents are not getting a square deal at home, while they are asked to risk their lives abroad. Has the minister given consideration to that phase of the matter, as it affects the war effort?

I do not wish to accept the minister's statement. I would call to his attention the fact that British Columbia was the first province to accept responsibility of taking care of what we thought old age pensioners needed. I had something to do with that, myself, because in conference with members of the provincial government I pointed out I did not think we would get in war time an expansion of the old age allowance from the federal government. Therefore do not lecture me about failing to recognize the responsibilities of the provinces.
I appreciate the danger of inflation and the danger of withdrawing from the war effort something that can be sacrificed from civilian use, thereby making a contribution to the war effort. But some of the things the government has done have helped the war effort immensely. The increase in the pay of the soldiers, which applies in Canada as well as overseas, increased the spending power of our soldiers. The amount involved there, is much more than would be needed to place old age pensioners in a category in which they could be cared for under the changed conditions of war. The increase this government has made with respect
Supply-Finance

to dependents' allowances has also increased spending power in Canada. But these things were never treated or recognized as factors which would reduce Canada's war programme. On the contrary they were things done by the government which strengthened enormously the war programme of the nation.
Let me say to the government, to-day when we are fighting for freedom let the word cross the seas to the Canadians in the armed forces; let the word go out to Canadians throughout this land that, notwithstanding the burdens we are carrying, we as a national parliament are prepared to guarantee not only that we shall give everything to the winning of the war, but that we shall give something to the well-being of our own Canadians in need. That will not interfere with our war effort at all.
In the discussion of every issue on domestic policy let us not raise this question or make the suggestion that all Canadians need to be reminded that the winning of the war is their responsibility. Every Canadian knows that. There has been no sacrifice yet asked to which Canadians have not willingly responded. I agree with the minister that not a penny should be spent that can be avoided. But when we say we must deny the old age pensioner a fair standard of living, a minimum subsistence allowance, and pay at the same time bonuses to the men who are working for wages they never had before, then that smacks of a type of impartial justice which is not the type of impartial justice for which we are fighting.
Yes, the minister has the support of every member of the house and every citizen in Canada in the work he is doing. But let us not overlook the fact that as we carry on the war there are some domestic obligations which have to be fulfilled at the same time.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The hon. member has spoken about dependents' allowances, and the increased pay to soldiers. That was our responsibility, and goodness knows we have enough of things that are our responsibility. And we try to discharge our responsibility in the field where it is clearly our responsibility. But the point I was making was that the other was primarily a responsibility which the provinces should discharge.

I rise to make one or two suggestions to the minister. In the course of his remarks he spoke about responsibility, and asserted that federal responsibility went only as far as contributions made to assist the provinces in meeting the cost of old age pensions. I would remind the minister of somethnig he well knows, namely, that the 
Old Age Pensions Act is a federal act, and that all the regulations in relation thereto are laid down by the dominion government. Federal government representatives are in the provinces to check every application submitted on behalf of old age pensioners.
In November, 1941, the minister asserted that payments made to old age pensioners were adequate inasmuch as the cost-of-living index in 1927-2S was in excess of what it was in 1941. But at that time he overlooked the fact that no one in 1927 or 1928 argued that the amounts paid at that time were adequate. It was stated that since this was a new adventure we must proceed with caution. It has been our bitter experience not only in respect of the Old Age Pensions Act but in respect of other acts that when payments have been made much lower than were considered adequate because the scheme was in an experimental stage we have lived to regret those low payments. I am not impressed unduly by the impassioned discourses of the minister when he takes exception to a matter of this kind. I contend that our war effort cannot be completely successful unless we give the fullest possible considers tion to all classes of the people in our community and see that justice and equality of sacrifice prevail.
It cannot be asserted and substantiated that these payments to old age pensions, which range from between $11 and $12 to S25 a month, ever were or much less are adequate at the present time. Not only that; we have described the discrepancy which exists between the single and the married old age pensioner whose wife is not old enough to qualify. The single man of seventy years of age may have his application for old age pension granted, and he may receive the maximum of $25 a month. But the married man of seventy years of age, whose wife may be anywhere between fifty and seventy years of age, receives no increase in his pension because he is married. That is rank inequality.
In connection with dependents' allowances and assigned pay, I contend that these should have absolutely no effect upon the payment of old age pensions. It is appalling even to consider that our government is doing that. I know what effect it is having on many of our boys overseas, and I know what effect it is having upon unity in this country. The minister asserted-I think he later made a correction-that where assigned pay alone is being paid, no deduction is made in the pension, but that where assigned pay and dependents allowance is being paid, they are both regarded as income. I contend that neither should be regarded as income in connection with the payment of old age pensions.

Supply-Finance
When it comes to making an expenditure apart from old age pensions, or when it comes to granting a cost-of-living bonus to men who are getting S2,000 or $2,100 a year, there does not seem to be any danger of the economy of Canada being jeopardized; but when we appeal for S5 or $10 additional for our old age pensioners, just because it does not happen to be the government policy we are told that we are ruining the economy of the whole country. That is pure rot. We have to face up to this question, and we have to face up to it soon. It is only by doing so that we can establish the degree of unity which this government believes, or which it has stated at times exists in this country, but which many of us know does not exist. I urge once again that we accept our responsibility in this connection and make the payments to our old people to which we know they are entitled.

In the first place I wish to tell the Minister of Finance that I admire his patience. He follows the discussion in the house very attentively and gives answers to questions asked to the best of his ability, sometimes under the most difficult of circumstances. To-night I have listened to some of the speeches that have been made by hon. gentlemen. The hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard and the hon. member for Red Deer, who has just spoken, expressed some views with which I agree, and which I am sure are shared by many hon. members.
Mention has been made of old age pensions. In order to understand this we should go back to consider how old age pensions were instituted. In the first place it was not provincial legislation; the first act was dominion. It was only after that act was passed that it was offered to the provinces as bait to induce them to contribute on a fifty-fifty basis. Mr. Bennett increased the dominion contribution to seventy-five per cent; he did not increase it to 100 per cent because he knew that this was purely a provincial matter according to the constitution. There are many old people who receive a pension, and several of them have had their pensions cut quite drastically.
The hon. member for Red Deer was correct in his reference to assigned pay and allowances. A father is not entitled to an allowance except in special circumstances. This contribution by the state of an allowance is granted only when the soldier assigns one-half of his pay. The matter is subject to investigation by doctors who make a report. The soldier or the officer must contribute part of his pay before an allowance is granted. A bachelor, or even a spinster who is in the army and who is supporting parents or younger brothers and sisters is in exactly the same position as
the head of a family, but the allowance to the wife is higher. Where a father is sick and unable to support his family; where this burden is assumed by a young man in the army who was the supporter of his family before his enlistment, I do not see why the allowance should be less than it is to a soldier's wife and children. I think that is most unjust. This is one of the domestic problems the government must consider.
The minister has referred to his burden and the burden of the country, namely, the tremendous debt. He has also said something about pressure that comes from other quarters. I admit that if any minister is subject to pressure, it is undoubtedly the Minister of Finance. He has my deepest sympathy. There are cases where we admit that there is pressure, and there are other cases where the pressure is not known, although it may exist. Members of the House of Commons are very anxious to know where the pressure comes from in certain cases, especially in the case of lend-lease for this year and the gift of one billion dollars that was made to Great Britain last year. Did any member of the House of Commons exert pressure on the Minister of Finance and on the government at large to bring down such a financial policy, or rather did the pressure come from the Old Lady of Threadneedle street-the Bank of England? We do not know what is behind it, but it was after the visit of Sir John Dill to Ottawa that we were told that the government had adopted this new policy of a billion dollar gift to the United Kingdom.
I do not see how we can give a billion dollars to any other country when we have some of our own fellow citizens who are old and some who are sick and who have not enough to make both ends meet. It is a question of humanity. All those who have spoken for the aged have been speaking for the underdog, the man or the woman who perhaps they will never meet but who is suffering now on account of the cold and who may be suffering also the pangs of hunger. What has been said to-night will be reported to them and will bring comfort to them. This is a domestic problem that has to be solved. In a country like ours there is no reason why we should not look after our own, and I appeal not only to the fairness of the Minister of Finance but also to his good heart, and in appealing to him I am not using any pressure. I ask him to remember the old people of the Annapolis valley, with whom he has lived and whom he knows so well, old people who may be sick, old people who were formerly fishermen but who cannot go out in their boats any more because they are too
Supply-Finance

old. I ask him to think of them when he has to make a final decision. I congratulate all the hon. members who have spoken for the aged. They have spoken as true Canadians. They do not forget that those who live in this country must rely upon the parliament of Canada for help when they need it, and I am speaking not only of help for our civilian population but also of help for our army. I will go further, Mr. Chairman, and ask the minister to enunciate a new policy on behalf of our soldiers, who at times have to pay for their own meals. I ask him to make the allowance to soldiers' wives and children, soldiers' parents, brothers and sisters in all needy cases non-contributory. I mean by non-contributory that, in the future, soldiers-when I say soldiers I mean both the men and the women who assign their pay- will no longer have to assign a portion of their pay to those who are so dear to them and whom they supported until they enlisted in the army.

I do not know exactly
how this question of old age pensions got into the discussion to-night. It is a pity that year after year we should be discussing pensions of $20 a month for our aged people, and year after year come to the conclusion that we can find nothing more for them than $20 a month. When we estimate the value of $20 a month in the things that the old age pensioners need, some sort of shelter, food, some clothing and a few other odds and ends to make their life fairly comfortable, are we to say that the people of Canada-and remember that these things can be provided only by the people of Canada who work and produce them-cannot provide our aged people with these modest comforts of life? I think every member of the house should blush with shame to ask our aged people, who have given their lives to building up this country, to live on the paltry subsistence that can be procured for $20 a month.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The pension in British
Columbia is $25, is it not?
L agree. We are more generous in British Columbia than people are in other parts of the dominion. The further west you go, the more generous you find the people.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The pension has been raised in other provinces. Nova Scotia is proposing to make it $25.

I was a member of the city council of Vancouver some years ago, and I remember that a great many old age pen-
sioners who had no relatives or homes used to come to council and turn over their pension so that they could go into an old people's home that was kept up by the city. The $20 a month which they turned over to the city did not pay more than half the cost of their living in the old people's home. I remember on one occasion asking the man in charge of the home what effect staying in the home had on the health and life prospects of the inmates. He said that it added on the average ten years to their lives because, he said, "When they come in they are free from all worry." I often wonder why or how the government of the day came to the conclusion that $20 a month at seventy years of age was the proper amount for an old age pension.
Item stands.
Progress reported.
